report.summary: Reviewed chunk 5 of 5 of daedalus/kairos/worktree.py; all claims verified against code.
risks: _refs_containing | high | Case-insensitive comparison of ref names may cause spurious exclusions, retaining branches that could be deleted. | Clarify if case-insensitive matching is intentional and test with mixed-case refs.
reap_branches | medium | A crashed process leaves unverifiable records; leaked branches are never reaped. | Document that operator must manually clean up leaked branches or add a recovery mechanism.
commit_candidate | medium | Uses git add -A which stages all changes including untracked files; may commit unintended files. | Consider using git add --all or explicit paths.
has_changes | low | Uses git status --porcelain; output format may vary with git version. | Pin git version in requirements or test against multiple versions.

handoff.purpose: Implements reap_branches, commit_candidate, has_changes, and helper methods with trust model and claims.

symbols.name: reap_branches
symbols.note: Method of GitWorktreeManager; deletes branches only when both in-process allocation and git's reachability confirm safety.

symbols.name: _forget_allocation
symbols.note: Removes allocation from in-memory dict and discards on-disk record.

symbols.name: _report_unverifiable_records
symbols.note: Returns list of on-disk records not vouched for; never acts on them.

symbols.name: _refs_containing
symbols.note: Returns list of refs (excluding given branch) that contain a given SHA.

symbols.name: _delete_unused_branch
symbols.note: Deletes a branch using -d then -D if needed, after re-verifying tip.

symbols.name: commit_candidate
symbols.note: Commits all changes in an allocated worktree.

symbols.name: has_changes
symbols.note: Returns True if worktree has uncommitted changes.

claims.text: An earlier version enumerated <worktree_root>/.daedalus-alloc/*.json and believed what it read. That made the ATTACKER the author of the entire input set... Two forged records naming real branches at their current tips were enough to delete feature/six-months-of-work and release-2.0, each with a printed reason that was false
claims.why: The current implementation does not read on-disk records; it uses in-memory _allocations and git's output, preventing the described attack.

claims.text: Candidate code runs as THIS user with THIS user's privileges, so there is no on-disk secret it cannot read and no on-disk file it cannot write. An authenticated record is therefore not available at this layer
claims.why: The code relies only on in-memory state and git's own data, not on on-disk secrets.

claims.text: a branch is deleted only when BOTH hold: 1. THIS manager object allocated it, in THIS process (_allocations, written by create_worktree), its worktree has been through cleanup_worktree, and its tip is byte-identical to the sha this manager itself read from git at allocation time. Nothing on disk contributes to this. 2. Some OTHER ref still contains that tip, so deleting the branch orphans no commit. This is git's answer, not ours
claims.why: The code checks _allocations[key] for branch_tip_at_creation and worktree_removed, and calls _refs_containing to verify other refs contain the tip.

claims.text: a branch leaked by a CRASHED run is never reaped, because the process that could vouch for it is gone. Records left on disk are reported as unverifiable and acted on by nobody. A leaked ref is cheap; a deleted branch is not.
claims.why: Report_unverifiable_records returns records not in _allocations but never deletes branches based on them.

claims.text: Returns: One dict per allocation examined, with branch, action (deleted / retained / absent / pending / unverifiable) and reason.
claims.why: The code builds report list with those keys and actions.

claims.text: Raises: RuntimeError: If any branch that was cleared for deletion could not be deleted. Every allocation is still examined first; the failures are reported together rather than aborting on the first one.
claims.why: The code collects failures in a list and raises RuntimeError at the end with all failures joined.

claims.text: Name the on-disk records nobody vouched for. Never acts on them. Reported rather than ignored so the leak is visible; reported WITHOUT any field parsed out of the file, because every byte in it is candidate-writable and echoing a forged branch name back at an operator as though it meant something is how the previous version printed false reasons.
claims.why: The method only returns record file names; it does not parse any fields from the files.

claims.text: Refs OTHER than refs/heads/<excluding> whose history holds sha. The one input to the reap decision that no candidate can forge. If this is non-empty, deleting the branch cannot orphan a commit. If it is empty the branch is the only thing holding that history, and holding history is exactly what this method must never destroy.
claims.why: The method uses git for-each-ref --contains sha and filters out the excluded ref.

claims.text: A FAILED CALL IS NOT AN ANSWER. git being missing, the repository being locked, .git being written by something else, a candidate that exhausted the handle table -- none of those is evidence that the tip is held elsewhere, so none of them may license a delete.
claims.why: The except clause catches RuntimeError and returns an empty list, retaining the branch.

claims.text: Compared case-INSENSITIVELY although git refs are case-sensitive: the only effect of a spurious match is that a ref is dropped from the holder list, which retains the branch. Erring toward retention is the correct direction for a method whose failure mode is deleting work.
claims.why: The code uses .casefold() for comparison, which is case-insensitive.

claims.text: Delete a branch already PROVEN to hold nothing but its base commit. -d is tried first so git's own merged-check applies. If git refuses anyway -- it compares against the current HEAD, which may have moved somewhere unrelated -- the sha proof (re-taken here, so the branch cannot have moved in between) is what authorises -D. The force flag is never reached without that proof.
claims.why: The method tries git branch -d first; if it fails, re-verifies tip and uses -D only if tip matches proven_tip.

claims.text: Commits all changes in the specified worktree. The path is proven to be an allocated worktree first: a swapped directory would otherwise turn git add -A + git commit into a commit of the developer's working tree.
claims.why: The method calls _require_allocated_worktree before running git commands.

claims.text: Return whether the candidate worktree differs from its HEAD.
claims.why: The method runs git status --porcelain and returns bool of output.

observations.what: _refs_containing uses case-insensitive comparison of ref names; git refs are case-sensitive. This may cause a ref to be incorrectly excluded from the holder list, leading to retention of a branch that could be deleted.

reap_branches does not handle the case where _allocations[key] lacks 'branch_tip_at_creation' key; it uses .get() and checks 'not expected', but if the key is missing, expected is None, and the branch is retained. This is safe but may retain branches that could be deleted.
commit_candidate uses git add -A which stages all changes, including untracked files. This may commit unintended files if the worktree contains untracked generated files.
has_changes relies on git status --porcelain output format; if git changes output format, the function may break.
